newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid worker plan repatriation of Zaire refugees.
newsitem.headline: Aid worker plan repatriation of Zaire refugees.

text.p: Relief workers plan to start repatriating Rwandan Hutu refugees from Zaire's once teeming Tingi Tingi camp on Monday but they say prospects for those driven further west by a relentless rebel advance look bleak.

"On Monday, there will be the first repatriations from Tingi Tingi," Corinne Perthuis, spokeswoman of the U.N. refugee agency, told a Kinshasa news conference after being evacuated from Zaire's third city of Kisangani.
Tingi Tingi, about 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani, housed 170,000 refugees before most fled the rebel advance. Only the weak or sick -- about 1,000 people -- stayed behind.
Perthius and other aid workers who were whisked out of Kisangani by French paratroops before rebels took the city on Saturday, said tens of thousands of frightened refugees had fled west.
As many as 150,000 Hutus were in Ubundu, clustered on the banks of the Zaire River 100 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani. Perthius said as many more were missing in the jungle.
Red Cross officials said around a third on the Hutus in Ubundu were seriously ill with malaria or diarrhoea and had raw feet from days of marching through the forests.
The refugees, including some armed Hutu extremists blamed for the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda, have trekked from camp to camp since the Tutsi-led rebels took up arms in October.
The fall of Kisangani left them squeezed beside the wide river, with their only means of escape from the rebels to cross to the western bank, a treacherous journey.
"They would prefer to die in the river than be with these rebels," said Clae Gratti, who led the International Red Cross Federation team in Kisangani.
Many of the armed Hutus seem now to have abandoned the refugees they controlled in earlier camps and Gratti said he saw no obvious sign of them in Ubundu.
He said refugees, many of them children on their own, were trying to cross the river on flimsy bamboo rafts covered in aid-agency plastic sheeting from their camps.
His staff watched powerless as a flotilla of about 30 such boats, with around six people on each, swept downstream to lethal rapids and presumed death during a storm on Thursday.
Other aid workers spoke of refugees fatally stranded on rocks upstream from waterfalls.
Perthius said more misery lay in store for those who managed to cross the river onto the western side, in the inaccessible and remote heart of Africa's third largest country.
"They may head to Opala. That is 200 km (120 miles) west from Ubundu. It would be very difficult for the refugees to move through the marshland and forest," she said.
She said food would run out and airdrops in such a forested area would be problematic, adding that the best solution might be for the refugees to stay put.
The humanitarian organisations pledged to do their best to reestablish contact with the refugees in Ubundu, perhaps through rebel-held areas.
